title: A 28nm 18.1μJ /Acquisition End-to-End GPS Acquisition Accelerator with Energy-Accuracy-Driven Mixed-Radix IFFT and ROM-Assisted Computing
problem: GPS receiver acquisition is the most energy-consuming task in mobile GNSS receivers, requiring correlation of multi-satellite signals across Doppler range and code delay space. Conventional implementations perform full IFFT/FFT per satellite at high precision, consuming significant energy; accuracy-vs-energy tradeoff is not exploited during algorithm optimization.
motivation: Mobile and IoT devices demand ultra-low-power GNSS acquisition for location services without draining battery; energy efficiency per acquisition is critical.
method: The accelerator reduces energy by using different precision levels at different stages of GPS acquisition. In early stages—Doppler and code-delay estimation, where you're narrowing down which satellite and at what timing the signal is—lower precision is acceptable. The chip skips expensive calculations by using ROM-assisted computing: precomputed lookup tables stored in read-only memory. It combines a dual numerically controlled oscillator (NCO, which generates reference signals), a mixed-radix FFT engine (a signal transformer that breaks down complex calculations), and a correlator (which matches received signals to references), all built at 28nm in CMOS technology with adaptive word-widths.
key_novelty: The accelerator exploits the fact that GPS acquisition stages don't all need the same precision, using lower precision early on and precomputed lookup tables to cut energy while still detecting satellites as accurately as existing methods.
contributions: 18.1 μJ per acquisition in 28nm technology (measured end-to-end including all signal processing)
Mixed-radix IFFT with energy-driven precision scaling improves efficiency vs. fixed-precision FFT
ROM-assisted computing eliminates expensive multipliers in low-precision stages
Integrated dual-NCO and correlator in single accelerator for parallel satellite search
limitations: Acquisition time (search latency), false alarm rate, and scaling to future GNSS constellations not discussed.
